Vidura
------------------------------------------
During the महाभारत period, the practice of नियोग or levirate was quite common. Since the king Vicitravīrya died suddenly without issues, the sage Vyāsa—as per the command of his मोथेर् Satyavatī—raised three children on the two queens अम्बा and अम्बिका as also the latter’s maid. विदुर was the maid’s son.
Though born of a śūdra मोथेर्, विदुर was saintly by nature. He proved to be better than भीष्म and Droṇa by refusing to fight for the Kauravas since they had transgressed all limits of धर्म.
He was said to be born out of an aṁśa (a part) of the glory of Lord यम, the deity supervising over the death and धर्म of the people of this world of mortals.
Throughout his life, he not only observed धर्म (righteousness) in his personal life but also taught and warned others about the right path.
The following are some of the more important aspects of his life: warning the Pāṇḍavas in a secret language about the dangers of the palace at Varaṇāvata built of inflammable materials; advising धृतराष्ट्र (father of the Kauravas) many times against his conduct of blindly supporting his sons even in unholy acts; entertaining कृष्ण with great devotion in his होउसे when he suddenly appeared after he had arrived in हस्तिनापुर for peace parleys; leaving on a पिल्ग्रिमगे just before the कुरुक्षेत्र war, to avoid taking part in it; departing for the forest along with धृतराष्ट्र and ultimately dying in the forest fire.
Viduranīti, the teaching imparted by विदुर to धृतराष्ट्र (vide महाभारत, Udyogaparva
-40) has now become a classic on एथिच्स्.

vidyādvāra
(‘doors of knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Vidyā or knowledge cannot be given to any and every person. There are rules and restrictions regarding imparting it to others.
According to one version the following six persons are vidyādvāras or those fit to receive it: a brahmacāri residing in the गुरु’s होउसे; one who is eager to learn and is prepared to pay the fees; one who is intelligent enough to understand well; one who is learned in the वेदस् and wants to learn other sciences; one who is dear (like a son or a friend, but having the capacity to receive the knowledge); one who is prepared to exchange his specialised knowledge for another field of knowledge.

Vidyādharas
(‘those endowed with the knowledge [of magical spells]’)
------------------------------------------
Like किम्पुरुषस् and किन्नरस्, the विद्याधरस् also are a class of celestial beings. They are said to reside in the Himālayan regions. Skilled in several arts and sciences and endowed with magical powers, they are devotees of शिव.
Iconographical texts show them as dark in colour, wearing red garments. They have two protruding tusks. In their two hands, they carry a गदा (mace) and a डमरु (hand-drum). The buffalo is their वाहन or mount.

Vidyāsūkta
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are considered a great treasure of knowledge and spiritual wisdom. They should be imparted only by a qualified teacher to a qualified student.
This is described in detail in the Nirukta (2.4), and is called Vidyāsūkta.
The following is a brief summary of the same:
The goddess of Vedic learning approached a learned ब्राह्मण and addressed him thus:
‘Protect me, because I am your wealth. Do not give me (impart my knowledge) to anyone who is jealous, who is not guileless and who has no self-control. Then only I will become very powerful. What you teach to your disciple must be pleasant to his ears. The disciple should consider his गुरु (teacher) as superior even to his own ड़थेर् and मोथेर्; and, should never hate him. One who dishonours his गुरु can never reap the benefits of knowledge. Teach me to one who is pure, not careless, is endowed with ब्रह्मचर्य (continence) and is intelligent; and never to one who dislikes you.’

No country can have peace and progress unless ruled by a balanced combi-nation of kṣāttratejas (kingly power) and brāhmatejas (saintly guidance). The former can degenerate into tyranny without the latter. And, the latter becomes impotent without the protection of the former.
Vidyāraṇya was one of the three brightest स्तर्स् that have adorned the horizon of Hindu India who have proved this, the other two being कौटिल्य (321 B. C.) and Samartha रामदास (A.
as the eldest son of Māyaṇa and Śrīmatī, Mādhava or Mādhavācārya—that was his premonastic name—was educated by his ड़थेर् first, and later by Vidyātīrtha (d. A.

).
Moved by the pitiable condition of the contemporary society which had been battered by the repeated invasions of the Muslim marauders and their savagery, विद्यारण्य discovered after a period of intense तपस् (austerity), the need to establish a purely Hindu kingdom under the heroic leadership of a suitable person. Fortunately for him, he was able to get the excellent assistance of two क्षत्त्रिय warrior-brothers—Hakka and Bukka—with whom as the nucleus he established the city of Vidyānagara or Vijayanagara. This developed, in course of time, into a glorious Hindu empire which lasted 230 years.
He continued to guide the ruler of the kingdom till his last days. His समाधि (tomb) is situated at the back of the विरूपाक्ष तेम्प्ले at हम्पि (in the Bellary district of Karnataka).
He was the pontiff of the Śṛṅgerī Śāradāpīṭha (one of the four monasteries established by शङ्कर [A.

.
In the post-शङ्कर period, he was one of the best exponents of Advaita philosophy.
His works are:
Pañcadaśī;Jīvanmuktiviveka; Anubhūtiprakāśa;Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha; Bṛhadāraṇyakavārttikasāra;Nṛsiṁha-uttaratāpanīya-upaniṣad-dīpikāParāśaramādhavīya;Sarvadarśanasaṅgrahaand Vaiyāsika-nyāyamālā.
His another, great, contribution was inspiring his younger brother Sāyaṇācārya (d. A.
) to compose detailed commentaries on all the four वेदस्, now well-known as the Vedārthaprakāśa.

Viduranīti
(‘ethical philosophy [taught by] विदुर’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata is like a vast ocean. It is believed that an ocean contains many gems. That is why it is also called ‘ratnākara’ (storehouse of gems). One of the bright gems or jewels of this great epic is विदुर.
After being convinced that war was inevitable between his sons and the Pāṇḍavas, धृतराष्ट्र sent सञ्जय (his charioteer) to the Pāṇḍavas with the message that they should abandon the path of war and retire to the forest. When he returned सञ्जय abused the blind king for his attitude of greed and the injustice meted out to the Pāṇḍavas. This strong reproach made him restless and sleepless the whole night. The very next morning, he sent for विदुर and confessed his state of मिन्द्. The advice that विदुर gave him forms the content of this work. It is spread over eight chapters in the Udyogaparva (Chapters 33 to 40). There are 588 verses in all.
Because the advice was given by विदुर, it is called Viduranīti. This section, treated as a subsection of the Udyoga-parva is also designated as Prajāgaraparva alluding to धृतराष्ट्र being awake (= prajāgara) the whole night due to restlessness.
A very brief summary of the contents may now be given here:
First Chapter (123 verses)
After spending a night without sleep, धृतराष्ट्र sends for विदुर who arrives immediately. विदुर first accuses the blind king of entertaining evil persons—Duryodhana, दुश्शासन, कर्ण and Śakuni—as his trusted lieutenants. He describes the characteristics of learned men and fools. He then expatiates on what ought to be done and what should be abjured, using the numbers one to ten in an intelligent and interesting manner. The last part of this chapter contains the advice of प्रह्लाद, the great king of the demons, to kings in general, quoted by विदुर.
Second Chapter (86 verses)
Dhṛtarāṣṭra confesses that he is upset and restless and seeks विदुर’s guidance. विदुर starts his discourses by saying that a true friend must give advice even if not solicited. In his long counsel, he stresses three things. Firstly, a king who wants to rule well, must know everything about his kingdom. Secondly, he should be neither miserly nor overgenerous. Thirdly, as a human being he should cultivate virtues that can make him great and avoid all vices. At the end he advises धृतराष्ट्र to hand over the reigns of the kingdom to Yudhiṣṭira, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas since he deserved it best.
Third Chapter (77 verses)
In this chapter विदुर illustrates by an ancient episode of Sudhanvan (a ब्राह्मण youth), विरोचन (a dānava prince) and his ड़थेर् प्रह्लाद (the king of the दानवस्) the superiority of the path of truth and justice. The rest of the chapter gives many principles of एथिच्स् including things that must be done and those which must be eschewed.
Fourth Chapter (74 verses)
This chapter starts with the advice given by the great sage दत्तात्रेय to देवस् (gods) and sādhyas (demigods). The sage stresses the importance of speech containing truth and sweetness. After narrating this, विदुर, in answer to a question by the blind king, expounds the qualities that should exist in a कुल or race to make it good and great. It is pure character that makes it good and great. He then describes the evils of anger and the importance of unity among the good.
Fifth Chapter (64 verses)
Vidura describes 17 types of persons as mūrkhas or foolish ones and advises that none should become a mūrkha. He then exhorts that good persons should be treated well and that the bad ones be repaid in their own coin!
When धृतराष्ट्र asks why a man’s life which should be of a hundred years’ duration is shortened, विदुर replies that it is the six evils like arrogance, uncontrolled anger or intense selfishness that shorten a person’s life. On the other hand, good persons who are obedient to the elders, who are devoted to God and who do not harm others and who practise other virtues like truth, live long.
Other points stressed by him are: importance of protecting oneself against अधर्म (unrighteousness); fair treatment of one’s dependents; qualifications of a right kind of dūta or messenger; five kinds of बल or strength like physical strength, economic power and power of wisdom; avoiding enmity with the great and powerful persons.
Sixth Chapter (47 verses)
In this chapter, the following topics are dealt with: treating the respected elders properly; avoiding persons of evil character; protecting women; how a king should select ministers who are trust-worthy; how he should behave towards his subjects and the enemies.
Seventh Chapter (85 verses)
Dhṛtarāṣṭra tries to counter विदुर’s sane advice by arguments of fatalism. विदुर replies that even the best advice given by a great person like बृहस्पति will fall on deaf ears if the receiver of the advice is prejudiced! He again exhorts the blind king to abandon his son Duryo-dhana and save the dynasty of the great Kurus.
Other pieces of advice rendered by विदुर can be summarised as follows: avoiding the evil ones who try to create misunderstandings among others; honouring and helping one’s jñātis or close relatives even if they are just ordinary persons; honouring the Pāṇḍavas by giving them their due; six factors like drinking or इग्नोरन्चे of the presence of the enemies nearby, to be avoided; cultivation of virtues like humility, heroism and forgiveness; characteristics of a good friend; importance of thoughts in shaping one’s character; on the acquisition of wealth by right means; looking upon others as one’s own self; the need to abandon greed.
Eighth Chapter (32 verses)
Vidura once again extols the greatness of धर्म. He then describes how āśā or desire which can never be satiated, destroys a person by pointing out the inevitability of death to all living beings. Since karma—good or bad—accompanies the spirit of the dead person, one should strive to acquire धर्म only. He concludes his discourse by describing briefly the duties of the four varṇas or castes.
It is rather tragic that धृतराष्ट्र while conceding the rightness of विदुर’s advice, confesses his weakness of his attachment to his son दुर्योधन which makes him go off the path! He ultimately resigns himself to his ‘diṣṭam’ or fate.
The Viduranīti can be considered a valuable treatise on general एथिच्स् even as the Bhagavadgītā is on spiritual wisdom.
The Bhāratabhāvadīpa of नीलकण्ठ चतुर्धर (14th century A. D.) is the only commentary available on this work.
See also VIDURA.

vidyā
(‘knowledge,’ ‘science’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the verbal root ‘vid’ (to know’) the term विद्या stands for knowledge in general as also for any organised body of knowledge.
The उपनिषद्स् divide विद्या into two varieties: aparāvidyā (lower knowledge comprising all worldly sciences including the वेदस्) and parāvidyā (spiritual wisdom resulting in God-experience). Sometimes, they have also used this word to indicate special modes of meditation such as Akṣipuruṣavidyā, Bhūmavidyā and so on.
Vidyā, when understood as ātmavidyā (realisation of the आत्मन्), is posited as the antidote of अविद्या or nescience.
The Arthaśāstra (2.1) of कौटिल्य (321 B. C.) recognises four kinds of विद्यास्: आन्वीक्षिकी (logic and metaphysics); trayī (the three वेदस् excluding the Atharva-veda); वार्त्ता (agriculture, trade and allied vocations); daṇḍanītī (statecraft).
The Viṣṇupurāṇa (3.6.28, 29) lists altogether 18 विद्यास् as follows: 4 वेदस्; 6 वेदाङ्गस्; Mīmāṁsā; न्याय; पुराणस्; धर्मशास्त्रस्; आयुर्वेद; धनुर्वेद; Gāndharvaveda; अर्थशास्त्र.
The 64 kalās (arts) are also sometimes known as विद्यास्.
See also VIDYĀS.

He was the son of गणपति Ṭhākūr and Haṁsinīdevī. Visapi—also called Gaḍavisapi—in the Darbhāṅga district of मिथिला in north Bihar was his native place. Educated by his ड़थेर् and later by one Harimiśra, he became a great scholar in Sanskrit as also in the local language called Maithilī.
He was an intimate friend of Śivasiṁha, the ruler of मिथिला.
Local legends say that Lord शिव, charmed by his poetical talents, worked as a servant—Uganā by name—in his होउसे!
During the last days, with the intention of dying on the bank of the river गङ्गा, he started on the journey in a palanquin. Though he died before reaching the river, it is said that the river itself changed its course and started flowing in the place where he passed away.
His works may be listed as follows:
1. Sanskrit works: Bhūparikramaṇa; Puruṣaparīkṣā; Śaiva-sarvasvasāra; Vibhāgasāra; Dānavākyāvalī and Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī.
2. Maithilī language: Padāvalī (songs); Gorakṣavijaya.
His songs in the Padāvalī are set to मुसिच् and are very popular. They breathe the spirit of devotion as also the love of the गोपीस् for कृष्ण.

vidyārambha
(‘commencement of learning [of the alphabet]’)
------------------------------------------
A child used to be sent to the गुरु-कुल for एदुचतिओन् after the उपनयन ceremony, generally at the age of seven. In the ancient days, the saṁskāra or sacrament of teaching the letters of the alphabet, perhaps, used to be conducted at the time of चौल (rite of hair-cutting for the first time) itself, usually at the age of five.
This saṁskāra, known as विद्या-rambha or अक्षराभ्यास, is quite common even now. It is being performed even at the age of three or four.
Orthodox tradition recommended the following procedure: fixing up an auspicious day, preferably in the उत्तरायण (northern solstice) period; bathing and decorating the child; propitiation of the deities गणपति, सरस्वती, नारायण, लक्ष्मी, बृहस्पति and the family deity; performance of a होम; teaching the alphabet to the child by first writing a मन्त्र such as oṁ namassiddhāya and then the alphabet; honouring the teacher.
Letters may be written on rice spread over a plate with the index finger. Later a slate and a suitable pen or chalk may be used.

Vidurāśvattha
(‘holy fig tree of विदुर’)
------------------------------------------
There is a huge pipal or holy fig tree (aśvattha) at the village Doḍḍakurugoḍu, about 6 kms. (4 miles) to the north of the town Gaurībidanūr in Kolar district (Karnataka State). As per the local legends it is the off-shoot of the original tree planted by विदुर, the minister of the Kauravas. The tree is on the right bank of the Pinākinī river and is surrounded by several small shrines dedicated to शिव, नारायण, नवग्रहस् and नागस् (stone icons of serpents).
The tree is worshipped as holy by the visiting pilgrims.
A big festival is held every year during चैत्र Pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day in the lunar month of चैत्र, usually in April) including the रथोत्सव (temple car festival).

Vidyās
(‘sciences’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Though the word विद्या normally means learning or knowledge, in a more technical sense it signifies a science or an art.
Indian philosophical thought has reached its acme in the उपनिषद्स्. Coming as a reaction to Vedic ritualism and priestcraft, it has to stress the need for realising the spiritual dimensions of man. The sages of the उपनिषद्स् with their deep insight into human nature, knew that a total break with the past would be rather difficult for the men steeped lifelong in rituals. Wishing to lead them to higher levels of spiritual experience, step by step, these sages devised several विद्यास् or upāsanas (mystic meditations) often based on the same rituals which they had practised.
These विद्यास् mentioned in the उपनिषद्स् and amplified to some extent by the commentators are sometimes listed as 32 in number. A few of them may now be considered here briefly.
1. Akṣipuruṣavidyā (‘science of the person in the eye’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15; 8.7.4)
Akṣipuruṣa means ‘the person in the eye’. He is identified with the आत्मन्. Obviously, he cannot be the reflection seen in the eyeball. He is the person who animates the eye and enables it to see. Or, he is the person seen through the inner eye, after purifying the मिन्द् through spiritual disciplines.
He is the द्रष्टा (the seer) and not the दृश्य (the seen). He is ब्रह्मन्.
Meditation on him as the seer is the Akṣipuruṣavidyā. The fruits of such meditation are believed to be obtaining all good things, shining in all the worlds and not being reborn after death.
2. Antarādityavidyā (‘science of the Person in the Sun’) (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2)
This refers to the पुरुष or the Cosmic Person in the orb of the sun. He is called tat (That) and satyaṁ (Truth). He is related to the person in the right eye of human beings (the जीव or the सोउल्), through his rays. When the time comes for the जीव to depart from the body he sees the sun without rays (like the full-मोओन्).
The earth (bhūḥ) and the sky (bhuvaḥ) are this Cosmic Person’s head and arms. The heavens (suvaḥ) form his feet. His secret name is ‘ahas’. One who knows thus, gives up and destroys sins.
3. Bhūmavidyā (‘science of the Bhūmā [the Great, Brahman>]’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23-26)
This is one of the most important sections of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The sage नारद approaches Sanatkumāra, considered a great teacher of spiritual wisdom of his times. Though नारद had mastered 19 sciences and fields of knowledge including the four वेदस्, he had not attained inner peace and tranquillity.
Sanatkumāra takes him step by step from lower meditations starting with nāma (name) as a symbol for ब्रह्मन् right up to Bhūmā, ब्रह्मन् itself. Though various fruits for these meditations have been predicated they are all inferior and not permanent. Only the knowledge of Bhūmā leads to the highest bliss and लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence. This is followed by a description of Bhūmā which is the same as the description of ब्रह्मन् as found in the उपनिषद्स्. One who realises it—the teacher declares—will be liberated from all bonds.
4. Daharavidyā (‘knowledge of [Brahman] in the small space [of the heart-lotus]’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1)
Daharavidyā deals with the meditation on ब्रह्मन् in the region of the heart, compared to a lotus containing a very small space (daharam puṇḍarīkaṁ). This आकाश (daharākāśa) is itself ब्रह्मन् containing the earth and the हेअवेन्, the sun and the मोओन्, lightning and स्तर्स्. Since the word आकाश is also a name of ब्रह्मन् (vide 8.14.1), this method of meditation on the daharākāśa is justi-fiable. As a result of this meditation leading to the realisation of the आत्मन् (or ब्रह्मन्) the sādhaka (the aspirant) will get whatever he wants.
5. Gāyatrīvidyā (‘knowledge of the गायत्री’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12 and 13)
This is a rather complicated विद्या or meditation dealt with in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Gāyatrī is an important Vedic metre, described as superior to other metres. It is manifested as vāk or speech and protects all bhūtas or beings. Since these beings are sheltered by पृथ्वी or the earth, गायत्री and पृथ्वी are identical. Man’s body including his heart, where his prāṇas or vital airs are situated, is also पृथ्वी, and hence the गायत्री.
The Vedic metre गायत्री has four pādas or quarters with six akṣaras or letters in each. These six letters can be considered as related to vāk (speech), भूत (beings), पृथ्वी (earth), śarīra (body), हृदय (heart) and प्राण (vital airs).
Puruṣa or ब्रह्मन् is the self of this गायत्री. He is to be meditated upon in the आकाश (or space) within the heart.
The Upaniṣad further explains how the पञ्चप्राणस् (the five vital airs) within the heart are related to आदित्य (the sun), चन्द्र (the मोओन्), अग्नि (the fire), parjanya (the air) and आकाश (the sky). Upāsanās or meditations on these in the prescribed manner will lead to several extraordinary results (ibid 3.1

).
6. Madhuvidyā (‘knowledge of the honey’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.1 to 11)
This विद्या (knowledge or meditation) is described in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.1 to 11). It is primarily connected with the upāsanā (meditation) on the आदित्य (the deity Sun) who is described as devamadhu or honey of the gods since he brings joy (like मधु or honey) to them.
Honey is stored in the honeycomb, in its chambers. The honeycomb is built up on a beam or any beamlike structure, by the honeybees. They collect honey from various flowers.
This analogy is now applied to आदित्य as follows:
Antarikṣa (sky) is the honeycomb. Dyuloka (heavenly regions) is the beam. Rays (of the sun) are the chambers or holes. Water particles in the rays are the small eggs (of the honey bees). The four Vedas—Ṛk, Yajus, Sāma and Atharva—are the bees. Vedic rituals are the flowers from which honey is collected. The results of performance of these rituals, viz., yaśas (fame), तेजस् (bodily lustre), indriya (vigour of the senses), vīrya (strength) and annādya (food) are all stored in आदित्य.
The various Vedic deities enjoy this honey in आदित्य with the more important ones as their leaders, as follows:
Eight वसुस् with अग्नि; Eleven Rudras with इन्द्र, Twelve Ādityas with वरुण; Twenty-one Maruts with सोम and Twelve Sādhyas with ब्रह्मा.
Any sādhaka (spiritual aspirant) who understands this and practises meditation as the deities did, will attain the same results as they got, ultimately realising ब्रह्मन् (ibid 3.12.3).
7. Pañcāgnivdyā (‘knowledge of the ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’) (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2 and Chāndogya Upaniṣad

)
The duly established Vedic fire has several parts like fire, fuel, smoke, blazing tongues, embers and sparks. Offerings of ghee or rice-cake are poured into it. This results in a specific fruit or product.
The ड़िवे ड़िरेस् mentioned in this Vidyā are: dyuloka (sky); parjanya (rain); लोक (this world); पुरुष (man); and, yoṣā (woman).
Various parts or acts which are connected with these are compared to the parts of fire and the oblation poured into it. Specific results are also assured if meditation is practised according to the directions given here.
It was taught by the king प्रवाहण जैवलि to the sage उद्दालक आरुणि, also known as गौतम.
8. Paryaṅkavidyā (‘knowledge of the couch or bedstead of हिरण्यगर्भ’) (Kauṣītaki ब्राह्मण Upaniṣad

)
This Vidyā is dealt with in the first chapter of the Kauṣītaki ब्राह्मण Upaniṣad.
Citra Gārgyāyaṇi wanted to perform a sacrifice. He chose गौतम आरुणि to be the chief priest and sent for him. गौतम, however, sent his son श्वेतकेतु instead. When the latter went to Citra, he was tested first with some questions which he was unable to answer. Since गौतम too was ignorant of the same, both he and his son श्वेतकेतु approached Citra as disciples to be instructed by him. What Citra taught them has now become known as Paryaṅkavidyā.
The Upaniṣad refers to the two well-known paths देवयान (or अर्चिरादि-मार्ग) and पितृयान (or Dhūmādimārga). When the जीव (individual सोउल्) reaches चन्द्र (the मोओन्) on his journey after death, he has to go beyond it by rejecting the offer of स्वर्ग (heavenly enjoyments) and start treading the path of देवयान. After passing through the various worlds of वायु, वरुण and so on, he reaches the world of हिरण्यगर्भ or ब्रह्मा.
Before reaching ब्रह्मा, this जीव has to cross the lake Āra, the river Virajā, enter the city of ब्रह्मा called Sālajja and then approach ब्रह्मा seated on the Paryaṅka (couch) in his palace Aparājita. After reaching him, the जीव ascends the Paryaṅka with one foot at first.
Then there is a long passage containing the conversation between ब्रह्मा and जीव.
Once the जीव reaches the world of ब्रह्मा and ascends the Paryaṅka he is liberated and will not return to mundane existence.
The Upaniṣad is full of descriptions which are highly symbolical.
This is Paryaṅkavidyā.
9. Prāṇāgnihotravidyā (‘knowledge of the अग्निहोत्र concerning the [five] prāṇas’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.19-24)
Agnihotra is a Vedic sacrifice to be performed daily by a द्विज (a member of the first three castes) who has established the Vedic fires. It is done more as a worship than for any specific results.
Prāṇāgnihotra is the act of eating food—converted into a mental sacrifice through contemplation.
A द्विज is expected to eat the first five morsels of ड़ोओद् as an offering to the five prāṇas such as प्राण, अपान and so on. If he contemplates this as offering oblations into the gastric ‘fire’ (power of digestion) known as the वैश्वानर-अग्नि, the result will be manifold. By this act not only is the body, along with the senses and the मिन्द्, satiated but also various aspects of nature such as the मोओन्, the fire, the earth, the sky, the rain and so on. The performer of this sacrifice will attain an excellent body and enjoys life with wealth and progeny.
This is known as Prāṇāgnihotravidyā.
10. Pratardanavidyā (‘knowledge imparted to प्रतर्दन [by इन्द्र]’) (Kauṣītaki ब्राह्मण Upaniṣad 3)
The king प्रतर्दन, son of Divo-dāsa, goes to the svargaloka (or हेअवेन्) by the dint of his powers. Pleased with it, इन्द्र the lord of svargaloka offers him a boon. प्रतर्दन requests इन्द्र himself to select a boon that is the best for human beings. Then इन्द्र teaches him, ‘Know me! That is the best for human beings!’
Indra has realised his identity with the आत्मन्, who is the mukhyaprāṇa (the chief life-force) and prajñā (pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्). Hence no evil or sin can ever taint him. One who meditates on him as प्राण and prajñā, lives for a long time here and then goes to the immortal world or attains इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
The mukhyaprāṇa and prajñā always go together and are inseparable. They depart together when the body dies. The word प्राण also indicates an indriya or sense-organ. As long as the mukhyaprāṇa remains in the body, the departure or loss of the other prāṇas or इन्द्रियस् does not result in the death of the body.
Ultimately, the mukhyaprāṇa and the prajñā (or prajñātmā) are one and the same. They are the same truth looked at from two different angles—the आत्मन्, which again, is ब्रह्मन्. He is आनन्द or bliss, who is beyond old-age and death. He is not affected by good or bad deeds. He is the Lord of the universe.
This विद्या is also known as

. Puruṣavidyā (‘knowledge of man as a sacrifice’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.16 and 17)
In this विद्या the life of a human being has been compared to a यज्ञ or sacrifice.
A सोमयाग (or सोम sacrifice) has three savanas (extraction of सोम juice), each of which is associated with a मन्त्र and a group of deities. By meditating on his life in the manner prescribed here, a man can attain good health and longevity of 116 years. This is puruṣayajña.
He should meditate on the first 24 years of his life as प्रातस्-सवन (morning-extraction) and his prāṇas (the vital airs and senses) as the gods known as वसुस्. If he gets any disease, he should pray to these वसुस् to join his life to the next सवन, the mādhyandinasavana, of 44 years thereby overcoming the disease and increasing the longevity.
He should then meditate on these 44 years as mādhyandinasavana (noon-extraction) and his prāṇas (vital airs) as the associated deities, the Rudras. If he falls sick during this period he should pray to these Rudras to join his life to the tṛtīyasavana (the third or evening extraction).
After this, he is advised to meditate on the next 48 years as the tṛtīyasavana (the third or final or evening extraction) as also the deities associated with it, the Ādityas. An earnest prayer to these Ādityas in case of illness will set things right.
The number of years (24, 44 and 48) is determined by the number of letters in the three mantras (in the metres गायत्री, triṣṭubh and जगती) used for extraction.
Mahidāsa ऐतरेय is said to have practised this विद्या and lived for 116 years.
12. Sadvidyā (‘knowledge of Sat or the highest Truth’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad

and 2)
This विद्या was taught to श्वेतकेतु by his ड़थेर् उद्दालक आरुणि.
In spite of undergoing a long course of training under a competent teacher, श्वेतकेतु did not know the fundamental truth by knowing which everything unknown becomes known.
Uddālaka states that it is Sat. In the beginning, before च्रेअतिओन्, Sat alone existed, the one without a second. It thought, ‘Let me become many. Let me reproduce myself.’ Then it evolved into this world through the three fundamental elements—fire, water and earth.
Sat or Sadvastu is the original funda-mental reality eternally existing.
This teaching is known as

. Saṁvargavidyā(‘knowledge of the ultimate substratum or absorbent’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1 to 3)
The teaching of the sage रैक्व to the king जानश्रुति Pautrāyaṇa has been designated as Saṁvargavidyā.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a noble king, well-known for his generosity, especially for distributing ड़ोओद् to the needy.
Once he heard from some swans flying over his palace that the greatness of a sage called रैक्व far exceeded his own. After a vigorous search, he was able to locate the sage sitting under a cart. He approached this sage रैक्व in a manner sanctioned by social conventions. Then रैक्व taught him the Saṁvarga-vidyā.
Saṁvarga means the ultimate substratum which absorbs everything into itself.
Vāyu (the cosmic air) is saṁvarga in the external world since अग्नि (fire), चन्द्र (moon), सूर्य (sun) and āpa (water) get absorbed into it at the time of dissolution.
Mukhyaprāṇa (the chief vital air) is saṁvarga in the body since in deep sleep the sense-organs and the मिन्द् get dissolved in it.
If one identifies the Mukhyaprāṇa with वायु and meditates on it as Virāṭ (the Cosmic Being), he is able to see (realise) everything that may be lying in the ten directions.
14. Śāṇḍilyavidyā (‘the knowledge taught by शाण्डिल्य’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14)
Brahman is designated here as taj-jalān since he is responsible for the च्रेअतिओन् (taj), dissolution (tal) and preservation or living, (tan) of this world. One has to meditate upon this ब्रह्मन्.
He is the same as the आत्मन् inside this body. He works through the मिन्द्. The प्राण or the chief life-force is his body. He is very subtle, resplendent, all-powerful, all-pervading even though bereft of all sense-organs.
He is in the heart and is subtler than the subtlest. He is also greater than the greatest since he is identical with ब्रह्मन्.
One who meditates upon him thus, attains him after the death of the body.
Thus declared the great sage शाण्डिल्य.
15. Udgīthavidyā (‘knowledge [or science] of the उद्गीथ’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1)
A सामन् is a ṛk or मन्त्र of the Ṛgveda set to the intonation system of the Sāmaveda. Its singing has several steps (called भक्ति) such as उद्गीथ, हिङ्कार, प्रस्ताव and so on.
In the singing of a सामन्, the उद्गीथ comes first and is sung by the उद्गातृ priest. It always begins with Oṁ. While chanting it, one should meditate upon परमात्मन्, considering it as his pratīka (word-symbol).
The उद्गीथ is the essence of सामन्.
One who meditates thus, is able to get the desires of the yajamāna (sacrificer) fulfilled.
This is Udgīthavidyā.
The entire first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is devoted to upāsanā (meditation) on the उद्गीथ in several ways and its results.
16. Upakosalavidyā (‘knowledge received by उपकोसल’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10 to 15)
Upakosala Kāmalāyana was a disciple of Satyakāma Jābāla. Though the teacher permitted his other disciples to return home after completing their एदुचतिओन् spread over twelve years, he did not allow उपकोसल to go back. In spite of his own wife requesting Satyakāma to teach उपकोसल, he ignored her and went away on tour.
Unable to bear this neglect, उपकोसल started ड़स्तिन्ग्. Taking pity on him the three Vedic fires—gārhapatya, anvāhāryapacana and āhavanīya—taught him first collectively, and then individually about ब्रह्मन्.
The gist of their teaching is as follows: प्राण (the chief life-force), kam (happiness) and kham (ākāśa or space) are ब्रह्मन्. It means the bliss of ब्रह्मन् one gets if one meditates on him as identified with the आत्मन् in one’s heart.
The fires then taught him about their identity with पृथ्वी (earth), आदित्य (sun), ap (water), चन्द्र (moon), आकाश (sky or space) and other cosmic phenomena. One who understands this, destroys all his sins, lives long and attains the world of अग्नि.
After returning home Satyakāma discovered that his disciple was shining brightly with knowledge. Learning from him that the Vedic fires had taught him, the teacher imparted the knowledge of the आत्मन् energising the senses like the eyes and his identity with ब्रह्मन् as also the result of this knowledge viz., attaining ब्रह्मलोक from which there is no return.
This has been termed Upakosala-vidyā.
17. Vaiśvānaravidyā (‘knowledge of वैश्वानर’) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11-18).
Five sages—Prācīnaśāla, Satyayajña, इन्द्रद्युम्न, Jana and Buḍila—started discussing about आत्मन् (individual सोउल्) and ब्रह्मन् (Cosmic Being) but could not come to any conclusion. Then they went to उद्दालक आरुणि for enlightenment. Since he too did not know, he took them all to the king अश्वपति Kaikeya.
Since they approached him as disciples in all humility, the king started teaching them.
In the ultimate analysis, आत्मन् and ब्रह्मन् are identical. They are called here by the name वैश्वानर.
When the king questioned them one by one, whom they were meditating upon as the वैश्वानर, they replied in different ways. The objects of their meditation were: dyuloka (heaven), आदित्य (sun), वायु (air), आकाश (sky or space), āpa (water) and पृथ्वी (earth).
Since वैश्वानर is the Cosmic Being enveloping the whole world and since these sages were meditating only on one limb or aspect of him, as if that represented the whole Being, their knowledge was partial and defective. The king अश्वपति Kaikeya then taught them about the true nature of वैश्वानर as the whole.
This is known as the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.
Conclusion
It is very difficult to comprehend these विद्यास् now and even more difficult to practise them. However, one can appreciate the role of the Vedic sages who tried to prepare the sādhakas (aspirants of spiritual life) to gradually switch over from a purely sacrificial religion to contemplation on the higher aspects of philosophy.
